Abū ʿUbayd preferred this, on the basis of the reading of Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn Wathhāb and others: *ʿāliyatahum*. Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation: Have you not seen a man wearing garments, with better ones over them? The rest of the readers read it with fatḥa on the *yāʾ*, as an adjective, meaning "above them," and this is the accusative of place (*naṣb ʿalā al-ẓarf*). It was also said: it is like His saying ﴿لاهِيَةً قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾ (their hearts are heedless). [[Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ: 3.]] We have already mentioned this, the placing of the adjective before the noun it describes. It was also said: the meaning is "high for them, its garments," like His saying ﴿هَدْياً بالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ﴾ (an offering reaching the Kaʿba) [[Sūrat al-Māʾida: 95.]] and similar.

﴿خُضْرٌ وَإِسْتَبْرَقٌ﴾: The readers differed about these. Ibn Kathīr, Abū Bakr, and al-Mufaḍḍal read *khuḍrin* in the genitive as a qualifier of *sundus*, and *istabraqun* in the nominative as a qualifier of *thiyāb*. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb read the reverse, and Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred it. Nāfiʿ, Ayyūb, and Ḥafṣ read both in the nominative. Yaḥyā, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read both in the genitive.

﴿وَحُلُّوا أَساوِرَ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾: *ṭahūr* means pure from defilements, which no hands have soiled and no feet have soiled, unlike the wine of this world. Abū Qilāba and Ibrāhīm said: this means it never becomes impure, but turns into a sweat in their hands like the scent of musk. A man of the people of Paradise is granted the appetite of a hundred men of this world, with their eating and craving. When he has eaten what he wishes, he is given a pure drink, which purifies his belly, and what he has eaten becomes a sweat that comes out of his skin, more fragrant than the pungent musk, and his belly shrinks, and his appetite returns. It was also said: it purifies them from sins, impurities, and filth, and makes them sweat for Paradise.

Jaʿfar said: He purifies them through it from everything other than Him, since nothing that has been soiled by the created world is pure.

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: their Lord gave them to drink upon the edge of the carpet of affection. He quenched them from the companionship of creatures and showed them the vision of the Real. Then He seated them upon the pulpits of holiness, greeted them with the greeting of the one who is consoled (*al-muzammil*), and rained down support upon them, so the valleys of longing flowed over them. He removed from them the cares of separation and greeted them with the joy of nearness.

I heard Abū al-Qāsim al-Ḥabībī say: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allah Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Shāshī say: I heard al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlawiyya al-Dāmaghānī say: Abū Yazīd al-Biṣṭāmī was asked about His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾. He said: He purified them through it from love for anything other than Him. Then he said: God has a drink which He has stored for His choicest servants. He Himself undertakes to give them to drink. When they drink, they become intoxicated; when they become intoxicated, they fly; when they fly, they arrive; and when they arrive, they are joined. ﴿فِي مَقْعَدِ صِدْقٍ عِنْدَ مَلِيكٍ مُقْتَدِرٍ﴾ (in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful).

I heard Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī say: I heard Abū Bakr al-Rāzī say: I heard Ṭayyib al-Ḥammāl say: I prayed behind Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah the ʿatama (night) prayer. He recited ﴿وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾, and began moving his mouth as if he were sucking. When he finished his prayer, he was asked: Are you drinking or reciting? He said: By God, if I did not find its pleasure in its recitation like my pleasure in drinking it, I would not have recited it.

Al-Ḥusayn told me, who said: Hārūn told us, who said: Ḥāzim ibn Yaḥyā al-Ḥulwānī told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmmār al-Mawṣilī told us, who said: ʿAfīf ibn Sālim told us, from Ayyūb ibn ʿUtba, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: A man from Abyssinia came to the Prophet (peace be upon him) asking him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "Ask and seek understanding."

He said: O Messenger of God, you have been preferred over us in appearance, colours, and prophethood. Tell me: if I believe in what you believe and act as you act, shall I be with you in Paradise? He said: "Yes." Then the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the whiteness of the black man will be seen in Paradise from a distance of a thousand years." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says: There is no god but God, has a covenant with God through it. And whoever says: Glory be to God and praise be to Him, a hundred thousand good deeds and twenty-four thousand good deeds are written for him."

A man said: How shall we perish after these, O Messenger of God?

He said: "A man will come on the Day of Resurrection, and if it were placed upon a mountain it would weigh it down. Then a blessing from the blessings of God, glory be to Him, will stand up and nearly consume all of that, unless God, exalted be He, shows him favour (*yatawwal*) through His mercy." [[According to Ibn Kathīr: *yataghammadahu* (covers him); according to al-Qurṭubī: *yalṭuf* (is gentle).]] He said: Then the verses were revealed: ﴿هَلْ أَتى عَلَى الْإِنْسانِ حِينٌ مِنَ الدَّهْرِ﴾ up to His saying ﴿وَمُلْكاً كَبِيراً﴾, the verses.

The Abyssinian said: And will my eyes see what your eyes see in Paradise?

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Yes." The Abyssinian then fell ill until his soul departed. Ibn ʿUmar said: I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) lower him into his grave with his own hand. [[Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr: 1/536, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/148.]]

﴿إِنَّ هذا كانَ لَكُمْ جَزاءً وَكانَ سَعْيُكُمْ مَشْكُوراً إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنا عَلَيْكَ الْقُرْآنَ تَنْزِيلًا﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: [It was revealed] in pieces, one verse after another, and He did not send it down all at once; that is why He said ﴿نَزَّلْنا﴾ (We sent down) ...

﴿فَاصْبِرْ لِحُكْمِ رَبِّكَ وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ آثِماً أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾: meaning "or ungrateful (*kafūran*)." The *alif* is an extension (*ṣila*). Al-Farrāʾ said: *aw* here carries the sense of [....] [[Illegible in the manuscript.]], like the saying of the poet:

*No grief of a bereaved mother is like my grief, nor the grief of a bereaved camel whose young has been lost to her.*

*Nor the grief of an old man who lost his she-camel on the day the pilgrims arrive and disperse.*

He meant: "nor the grief of an old man."

Qatāda said: *al-āthim* is *al-kafūr* (the ungrateful). God, exalted be He, forbade His Prophet from obeying Abū Jahl when the prayer was made obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ), while he was still in Makkah. Abū Jahl forbade him from it and said: If I see Muhammad praying, I will step on his neck. So God revealed this verse.

Muqātil said: ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ﴾ means from the polytheists of Makkah, that is ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): If you have done what you have done for the sake of women, Quraysh knows that my daughters are among the most beautiful. I will marry you to my daughter and bring her to you without a dowry, and you will return from this affair. [[Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/149, which has a continuation.]]

﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ means al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): O Muhammad, if you have done this for the sake of wealth, Quraysh knows that I am among the wealthiest of them. I will give you enough wealth to satisfy you, so return from this affair. God, exalted be He, then revealed ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ [آثِماً]﴾, meaning ʿUtba, ﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ meaning and not the ungrateful one, who is al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 76, verses 14–24:**

﴿وَدانِيَةً عَلَيْهِمْ ظِلالُها﴾ means: its shades, the shade of its trees, will be close to them. There are several views on the grammatical case (i'rab) of *dāniyatan*. First, it is coordinated (*'atf*) with the preceding word *muttaki'īna* (reclining). Second, it is coordinated with the position (*mawdi'*) of the phrase ﴿لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها شَمْساً﴾ (they will not see in it a sun), so that the sense is "and they will see [shades] close." Third, it is in the accusative of praise (*al-madh*). The feminine form *dāniyatan* is used because *ẓilāl* (shades) is a plural noun. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿūd), it is *wa-dāniyan ʿalayhim*, which places the verb first. In the codex of Ubayy, it is *wa-dānin*, in the nominative, as a new sentence (*isti'nāf*).

﴿وَذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلًا﴾: *dhullilat* means it was made subservient and brought near. *Quṭūfuhā* means its fruits, and *tadhlīlan* means in complete submission. They will eat from its fruits standing, sitting, and reclining, and they will reach them and take them however they wish, in whatever state they are in.

We were told by ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥāmid, who said: Ḥāmid ibn Muḥammad told us, who said: Mūsā ibn Isḥāq told us, who said: My father told us, who said: Sufyān told us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said: The land of Paradise is of silver (*warq*), its soil is musk, the roots of its trees are gold and silver, its branches are pearls, chrysolite and rubies, and the leaves and fruit are beneath that. Whoever eats standing will not be harmed, [and whoever eats sitting will not be harmed], and whoever eats reclining will not be harmed. That is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿وَذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلًا﴾.

﴿وَيُطافُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِآنِيَةٍ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ وَأَكْوابٍ كانَتْ قَوارِيرَا قَوارِيرَا مِنْ فِضَّةٍ﴾: The commentators said: He meant the whiteness of silver combined with the clarity of glass. Its clarity is that of glass, yet it is made of silver. [[Al-Muṣannaf of Ibn Abī Shayba: 8/67, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/139, at the verse.]]

We were told by Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥamdūn, who said: Makkī told us, who said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Bishr told us, who said: Sufyān told us. And ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥāmid told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ḥamdawayh told us, who said: Maḥmūd ibn Ādam told us, who said: Sufyān told us, from ʿAmr, from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿قَوارِيرَا مِنْ فِضَّةٍ﴾. He said: If you took silver from the silver of this world and beat it until you made it like the wing of a fly, you would not see the water behind it. But the glass of Paradise has the whiteness of silver and the clarity of glass.

Al-Kalbī and al-Thumālī said: God made the glass of each people from the soil of their land. The soil of Paradise is silver, so from that silver He made glasses for them to drink from. ﴿قَدَّرُوها تَقْدِيراً﴾ means they are measured according to their ranks, neither more nor less. Al-Rabīʿ and al-Qurṭubī said: according to the size of the palm. The common reading (*qirā'at al-ʿāmma*, the reading of the majority) has *qaddarahā* with fatḥa on the *qāf* and *dāl*, meaning that the cup-bearers who circulate among them measure it out for them.

Ibn Fanjawayh told me, who said: Ibn Shanba told us, who said: Abū Ḥāmid al-Mustamlī told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ḥātim al-Raqqī told us, who said: Hishām told us, who said: Ismāʿīl ibn Sālim told us, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: I heard him read it *quddirūhā* with *ḍamma* on the *qāf* and *kasra* on the *dāl*, meaning that it was measured out to them, so there is no excess or deficiency in it. He said: I also heard someone else read *qaddarūhā fī anfusihim* (they measured it in their own minds), so it came to them as they had measured it, neither more nor less.

﴿وَيُسْقَوْنَ فِيها كَأْساً كانَ مِزاجُها زَنْجَبِيلًا﴾: a drink of driving and delight, without intoxication. The Arabs favour ginger (*zanjabīl*), and their poet said:

*As if a jinn of ginger had mixed*
*its taste into her mouth, and a fragrant, spreading wine* [[Kitāb al-ʿAyn of al-Farāhīdī: 6/280. The verse is by al-Aʿshā.]]

It was also said: it is a spring in Paradise from which one tastes the flavour of ginger.

Qatāda said: The muqarrabūn (those brought near) drink it pure, and it is mixed for the rest of the people of Paradise.

﴿عَيْناً فِيها تُسَمَّى سَلْسَبِيلًا﴾: Qatāda said: *salsabīl* means smooth, submissive to them; they direct it wherever they wish. Mujāhid said: it is a fast-flowing stream. [[Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī: 29/271, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: (19/142), where it reads: fast-flowing, flowing into their throats with ease.]] Yamān said: it is good in taste and flavour. The Arabs say: this is a smooth (*salis*) and *salsal* and *salsabīl* drink. Abū al-ʿĀliya and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said: it was named *salsabīl* because it flows smoothly over them in the paths and in their dwellings. It springs from the root of the Throne, from the Garden of Eden, to the people of the gardens, with the coldness of camphor, the taste of ginger, and the scent of musk. The meaning of *tusammā* (is named) is "is described," because most scholars hold that *salsabīl* is a descriptive attribute of the name.

﴿وَيَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ وِلْدانٌ مُخَلَّدُونَ إِذا رَأَيْتَهُمْ حَسِبْتَهُمْ لُؤْلُؤاً مَنْثُوراً وَإِذا رَأَيْتَ ثَمَّ رَأَيْتَ نَعِيماً وَمُلْكاً كَبِيراً﴾. The meaning of *mulkan kabīran* is that the lowest of them in rank (meaning the people of Paradise) will look from his kingdom across a distance of a thousand years, and will see its farthest end as clearly as its nearest. It was also said: it is the angels' seeking permission to enter upon them. And it was said: *mulkan kabīran* means a kingdom that has no end.

Abū Bakr al-Warrāq said: a kingdom not followed by destruction. Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Tirmidhī said: it means the kingdom of creation (*mulk al-takwīn*): when He wills a thing, it is.

The Abyssinian said: And will my eyes see what your eyes see in Paradise?

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Yes." The Abyssinian then fell ill until his soul departed. Ibn ʿUmar said: I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) lower him into his grave with his own hand. [[Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr: 1/536, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/148.]]

﴿إِنَّ هذا كانَ لَكُمْ جَزاءً وَكانَ سَعْيُكُمْ مَشْكُوراً إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنا عَلَيْكَ الْقُرْآنَ تَنْزِيلًا﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: [It was revealed] in pieces, one verse after another, and He did not send it down all at once; that is why He said ﴿نَزَّلْنا﴾ (We sent down) ...

﴿فَاصْبِرْ لِحُكْمِ رَبِّكَ وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ آثِماً أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾: meaning "or ungrateful (*kafūran*)." The *alif* is an extension (*ṣila*). Al-Farrāʾ said: *aw* here carries the sense of [....] [[Illegible in the manuscript.]], like the saying of the poet:

*No grief of a bereaved mother is like my grief, nor the grief of a bereaved camel whose young has been lost to her.*

*Nor the grief of an old man who lost his she-camel on the day the pilgrims arrive and disperse.*

He meant: "nor the grief of an old man."

Qatāda said: *al-āthim* is *al-kafūr* (the ungrateful). God, exalted be He, forbade His Prophet from obeying Abū Jahl when the prayer was made obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ), while he was still in Makkah. Abū Jahl forbade him from it and said: If I see Muhammad praying, I will step on his neck. So God revealed this verse.

Muqātil said: ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ﴾ means from the polytheists of Makkah, that is ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): If you have done what you have done for the sake of women, Quraysh knows that my daughters are among the most beautiful. I will marry you to my daughter and bring her to you without a dowry, and you will return from this affair. [[Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/149, which has a continuation.]]

﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ means al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): O Muhammad, if you have done this for the sake of wealth, Quraysh knows that I am among the wealthiest of them. I will give you enough wealth to satisfy you, so return from this affair. God, exalted be He, then revealed ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ [آثِماً]﴾, meaning ʿUtba, ﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ meaning and not the ungrateful one, who is al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 76, verses 14–24:**

﴿وَدانِيَةً عَلَيْهِمْ ظِلالُها﴾ means: its shades, the shade of its trees, will be close to them. There are several views on the grammatical case (i'rab) of *dāniyatan*. First, it is coordinated (*'atf*) with the preceding word *muttaki'īna* (reclining). Second, it is coordinated with the position (*mawdi'*) of the phrase ﴿لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها شَمْساً﴾ (they will not see in it a sun), so that the sense is "and they will see [shades] close." Third, it is in the accusative of praise (*al-madh*). The feminine form *dāniyatan* is used because *ẓilāl* (shades) is a plural noun. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿūd), it is *wa-dāniyan ʿalayhim*, which places the verb first. In the codex of Ubayy, it is *wa-dānin*, in the nominative, as a new sentence (*isti'nāf*).

﴿وَذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلًا﴾: *dhullilat* means it was made subservient and brought near. *Quṭūfuhā* means its fruits, and *tadhlīlan* means in complete submission. They will eat from its fruits standing, sitting, and reclining, and they will reach them and take them however they wish, in whatever state they are in.

We were told by ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥāmid, who said: Ḥāmid ibn Muḥammad told us, who said: Mūsā ibn Isḥāq told us, who said: My father told us, who said: Sufyān told us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said: The land of Paradise is of silver (*warq*), its soil is musk, the roots of its trees are gold and silver, its branches are pearls, chrysolite and rubies, and the leaves and fruit are beneath that. Whoever eats standing will not be harmed, [and whoever eats sitting will not be harmed], and whoever eats reclining will not be harmed. That is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿وَذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلًا﴾.

﴿وَيُطافُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِآنِيَةٍ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ وَأَكْوابٍ كانَتْ قَوارِيرَا قَوارِيرَا مِنْ فِضَّةٍ﴾: The commentators said: He meant the whiteness of silver combined with the clarity of glass. Its clarity is that of glass, yet it is made of silver. [[Al-Muṣannaf of Ibn Abī Shayba: 8/67, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/139, at the verse.]]

We were told by Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥamdūn, who said: Makkī told us, who said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Bishr told us, who said: Sufyān told us. And ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥāmid told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ḥamdawayh told us, who said: Maḥmūd ibn Ādam told us, who said: Sufyān told us, from ʿAmr, from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿قَوارِيرَا مِنْ فِضَّةٍ﴾. He said: If you took silver from the silver of this world and beat it until you made it like the wing of a fly, you would not see the water behind it. But the glass of Paradise has the whiteness of silver and the clarity of glass.

Al-Kalbī and al-Thumālī said: God made the glass of each people from the soil of their land. The soil of Paradise is silver, so from that silver He made glasses for them to drink from. ﴿قَدَّرُوها تَقْدِيراً﴾ means they are measured according to their ranks, neither more nor less. Al-Rabīʿ and al-Qurṭubī said: according to the size of the palm. The common reading (*qirā'at al-ʿāmma*, the reading of the majority) has *qaddarahā* with fatḥa on the *qāf* and *dāl*, meaning that the cup-bearers who circulate among them measure it out for them.

Ibn Fanjawayh told me, who said: Ibn Shanba told us, who said: Abū Ḥāmid al-Mustamlī told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ḥātim al-Raqqī told us, who said: Hishām told us, who said: Ismāʿīl ibn Sālim told us, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: I heard him read it *quddirūhā* with *ḍamma* on the *qāf* and *kasra* on the *dāl*, meaning that it was measured out to them, so there is no excess or deficiency in it. He said: I also heard someone else read *qaddarūhā fī anfusihim* (they measured it in their own minds), so it came to them as they had measured it, neither more nor less.

﴿وَيُسْقَوْنَ فِيها كَأْساً كانَ مِزاجُها زَنْجَبِيلًا﴾: a drink of driving and delight, without intoxication. The Arabs favour ginger (*zanjabīl*), and their poet said:

*As if a jinn of ginger had mixed*
*its taste into her mouth, and a fragrant, spreading wine* [[Kitāb al-ʿAyn of al-Farāhīdī: 6/280. The verse is by al-Aʿshā.]]

It was also said: it is a spring in Paradise from which one tastes the flavour of ginger.

Qatāda said: The muqarrabūn (those brought near) drink it pure, and it is mixed for the rest of the people of Paradise.

﴿عَيْناً فِيها تُسَمَّى سَلْسَبِيلًا﴾: Qatāda said: *salsabīl* means smooth, submissive to them; they direct it wherever they wish. Mujāhid said: it is a fast-flowing stream. [[Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī: 29/271, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: (19/142), where it reads: fast-flowing, flowing into their throats with ease.]] Yamān said: it is good in taste and flavour. The Arabs say: this is a smooth (*salis*) and *salsal* and *salsabīl* drink. Abū al-ʿĀliya and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said: it was named *salsabīl* because it flows smoothly over them in the paths and in their dwellings. It springs from the root of the Throne, from the Garden of Eden, to the people of the gardens, with the coldness of camphor, the taste of ginger, and the scent of musk. The meaning of *tusammā* (is named) is "is described," because most scholars hold that *salsabīl* is a descriptive attribute of the name.

﴿وَيَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ وِلْدانٌ مُخَلَّدُونَ إِذا رَأَيْتَهُمْ حَسِبْتَهُمْ لُؤْلُؤاً مَنْثُوراً وَإِذا رَأَيْتَ ثَمَّ رَأَيْتَ نَعِيماً وَمُلْكاً كَبِيراً﴾. The meaning of *mulkan kabīran* is that the lowest of them in rank (meaning the people of Paradise) will look from his kingdom across a distance of a thousand years, and will see its farthest end as clearly as its nearest. It was also said: it is the angels' seeking permission to enter upon them. And it was said: *mulkan kabīran* means a kingdom that has no end.

Abū Bakr al-Warrāq said: a kingdom not followed by destruction. Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Tirmidhī said: it means the kingdom of creation (*mulk al-takwīn*): when He wills a thing, it is.

﴿عالِيَهُمْ ثِيابُ سُندُسٍ﴾: Qatāda, Mujāhid, Ibn Sīrīn, ʿAwn al-ʿUqaylī, Ibn Muḥayṣ, Abū Jaʿfar, Nāfiʿ, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza, and Ayyūb read *ʿāliyahum* with sukūn on the *yāʾ*, as a named noun described by the verb: *ʿalāhum*, so he is *ʿāliyahum*. Abū ʿUbayd preferred this, on the basis of the reading of Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn Wathhāb and others: *ʿāliyatahum*. Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation: Have you not seen a man wearing garments, with better ones over them? The rest of the readers read it with fatḥa on the *yāʾ*, as an adjective, meaning "above them," and this is the accusative of place (*naṣb ʿalā al-ẓarf*). It was also said: it is like His saying ﴿لاهِيَةً قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾ (their hearts are heedless). [[Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ: 3.]] We have already mentioned this, the placing of the adjective before the noun it describes. It was also said: the meaning is "high for them, its garments," like His saying ﴿هَدْياً بالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ﴾ (an offering reaching the Kaʿba) [[Sūrat al-Māʾida: 95.]] and similar.

﴿خُضْرٌ وَإِسْتَبْرَقٌ﴾: The readers differed about these. Ibn Kathīr, Abū Bakr, and al-Mufaḍḍal read *khuḍrin* in the genitive as a qualifier of *sundus*, and *istabraqun* in the nominative as a qualifier of *thiyāb*. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb read the reverse, and Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred it. Nāfiʿ, Ayyūb, and Ḥafṣ read both in the nominative. Yaḥyā, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read both in the genitive.

﴿وَحُلُّوا أَساوِرَ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾: *ṭahūr* means pure from defilements, which no hands have soiled and no feet have soiled, unlike the wine of this world. Abū Qilāba and Ibrāhīm said: this means it never becomes impure, but turns into a sweat in their hands like the scent of musk. A man of the people of Paradise is granted the appetite of a hundred men of this world, with their eating and craving. When he has eaten what he wishes, he is given a pure drink, which purifies his belly, and what he has eaten becomes a sweat that comes out of his skin, more fragrant than the pungent musk, and his belly shrinks, and his appetite returns. It was also said: it purifies them from sins, impurities, and filth, and makes them sweat for Paradise.

Jaʿfar said: He purifies them through it from everything other than Him, since nothing that has been soiled by the created world is pure.

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: their Lord gave them to drink upon the edge of the carpet of affection. He quenched them from the companionship of creatures and showed them the vision of the Real. Then He seated them upon the pulpits of holiness, greeted them with the greeting of the one who is consoled (*al-muzammil*), and rained down support upon them, so the valleys of longing flowed over them. He removed from them the cares of separation and greeted them with the joy of nearness.

I heard Abū al-Qāsim al-Ḥabībī say: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allah Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Shāshī say: I heard al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlawiyya al-Dāmaghānī say: Abū Yazīd al-Biṣṭāmī was asked about His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾. He said: He purified them through it from love for anything other than Him. Then he said: God has a drink which He has stored for His choicest servants. He Himself undertakes to give them to drink. When they drink, they become intoxicated; when they become intoxicated, they fly; when they fly, they arrive; and when they arrive, they are joined. ﴿فِي مَقْعَدِ صِدْقٍ عِنْدَ مَلِيكٍ مُقْتَدِرٍ﴾ (in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful).

I heard Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī say: I heard Abū Bakr al-Rāzī say: I heard Ṭayyib al-Ḥammāl say: I prayed behind Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah the ʿatama (night) prayer. He recited ﴿وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾, and began moving his mouth as if he were sucking. When he finished his prayer, he was asked: Are you drinking or reciting? He said: By God, if I did not find its pleasure in its recitation like my pleasure in drinking it, I would not have recited it.

Al-Ḥusayn told me, who said: Hārūn told us, who said: Ḥāzim ibn Yaḥyā al-Ḥulwānī told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmmār al-Mawṣilī told us, who said: ʿAfīf ibn Sālim told us, from Ayyūb ibn ʿUtba, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: A man from Abyssinia came to the Prophet (peace be upon him) asking him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "Ask and seek understanding."

He said: O Messenger of God, you have been preferred over us in appearance, colours, and prophethood. Tell me: if I believe in what you believe and act as you act, shall I be with you in Paradise? He said: "Yes." Then the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the whiteness of the black man will be seen in Paradise from a distance of a thousand years." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says: There is no god but God, has a covenant with God through it. And whoever says: Glory be to God and praise be to Him, a hundred thousand good deeds and twenty-four thousand good deeds are written for him."

A man said: How shall we perish after these, O Messenger of God?

He said: "A man will come on the Day of Resurrection, and if it were placed upon a mountain it would weigh it down. Then a blessing from the blessings of God, glory be to Him, will stand up and nearly consume all of that, unless God, exalted be He, shows him favour (*yatawwal*) through His mercy." [[According to Ibn Kathīr: *yataghammadahu* (covers him); according to al-Qurṭubī: *yalṭuf* (is gentle).]] He said: Then the verses were revealed: ﴿هَلْ أَتى عَلَى الْإِنْسانِ حِينٌ مِنَ الدَّهْرِ﴾ up to His saying ﴿وَمُلْكاً كَبِيراً﴾, the verses.

The Abyssinian said: And will my eyes see what your eyes see in Paradise?

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Yes." The Abyssinian then fell ill until his soul departed. Ibn ʿUmar said: I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) lower him into his grave with his own hand. [[Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr: 1/536, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/148.]]

﴿إِنَّ هذا كانَ لَكُمْ جَزاءً وَكانَ سَعْيُكُمْ مَشْكُوراً إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنا عَلَيْكَ الْقُرْآنَ تَنْزِيلًا﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: [It was revealed] in pieces, one verse after another, and He did not send it down all at once; that is why He said ﴿نَزَّلْنا﴾ (We sent down) ...

﴿فَاصْبِرْ لِحُكْمِ رَبِّكَ وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ آثِماً أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾: meaning "or ungrateful (*kafūran*)." The *alif* is an extension (*ṣila*). Al-Farrāʾ said: *aw* here carries the sense of [....] [[Illegible in the manuscript.]], like the saying of the poet:

*No grief of a bereaved mother is like my grief, nor the grief of a bereaved camel whose young has been lost to her.*

*Nor the grief of an old man who lost his she-camel on the day the pilgrims arrive and disperse.*

He meant: "nor the grief of an old man."

Qatāda said: *al-āthim* is *al-kafūr* (the ungrateful). God, exalted be He, forbade His Prophet from obeying Abū Jahl when the prayer was made obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ), while he was still in Makkah. Abū Jahl forbade him from it and said: If I see Muhammad praying, I will step on his neck. So God revealed this verse.

Muqātil said: ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ﴾ means from the polytheists of Makkah, that is ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): If you have done what you have done for the sake of women, Quraysh knows that my daughters are among the most beautiful. I will marry you to my daughter and bring her to you without a dowry, and you will return from this affair. [[Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/149, which has a continuation.]]

﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ means al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): O Muhammad, if you have done this for the sake of wealth, Quraysh knows that I am among the wealthiest of them. I will give you enough wealth to satisfy you, so return from this affair. God, exalted be He, then revealed ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ [آثِماً]﴾, meaning ʿUtba, ﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ meaning and not the ungrateful one, who is al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.

Ibn Fanjawayh told me, who said: Ibn Shanba told us, who said: Abū Ḥāmid al-Mustamlī told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ḥātim al-Raqqī told us, who said: Hishām told us, who said: Ismāʿīl ibn Sālim told us, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: I heard him read it *quddirūhā* with *ḍamma* on the *qāf* and *kasra* on the *dāl*, meaning that it was measured out to them, so there is no excess or deficiency in it. He said: I also heard someone else read *qaddarūhā fī anfusihim* (they measured it in their own minds), so it came to them as they had measured it, neither more nor less.

﴿وَيُسْقَوْنَ فِيها كَأْساً كانَ مِزاجُها زَنْجَبِيلًا﴾: a drink of driving and delight, without intoxication. The Arabs favour ginger (*zanjabīl*), and their poet said:

*As if a jinn of ginger had mixed*
*its taste into her mouth, and a fragrant, spreading wine* [[Kitāb al-ʿAyn of al-Farāhīdī: 6/280. The verse is by al-Aʿshā.]]

It was also said: it is a spring in Paradise from which one tastes the flavour of ginger.

Qatāda said: The muqarrabūn (those brought near) drink it pure, and it is mixed for the rest of the people of Paradise.

﴿عَيْناً فِيها تُسَمَّى سَلْسَبِيلًا﴾: Qatāda said: *salsabīl* means smooth, submissive to them; they direct it wherever they wish. Mujāhid said: it is a fast-flowing stream. [[Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī: 29/271, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: (19/142), where it reads: fast-flowing, flowing into their throats with ease.]] Yamān said: it is good in taste and flavour. The Arabs say: this is a smooth (*salis*) and *salsal* and *salsabīl* drink. Abū al-ʿĀliya and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said: it was named *salsabīl* because it flows smoothly over them in the paths and in their dwellings. It springs from the root of the Throne, from the Garden of Eden, to the people of the gardens, with the coldness of camphor, the taste of ginger, and the scent of musk. The meaning of *tusammā* (is named) is "is described," because most scholars hold that *salsabīl* is a descriptive attribute of the name.

﴿وَيَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ وِلْدانٌ مُخَلَّدُونَ إِذا رَأَيْتَهُمْ حَسِبْتَهُمْ لُؤْلُؤاً مَنْثُوراً وَإِذا رَأَيْتَ ثَمَّ رَأَيْتَ نَعِيماً وَمُلْكاً كَبِيراً﴾. The meaning of *mulkan kabīran* is that the lowest of them in rank (meaning the people of Paradise) will look from his kingdom across a distance of a thousand years, and will see its farthest end as clearly as its nearest. It was also said: it is the angels' seeking permission to enter upon them. And it was said: *mulkan kabīran* means a kingdom that has no end.

Abū Bakr al-Warrāq said: a kingdom not followed by destruction. Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Tirmidhī said: it means the kingdom of creation (*mulk al-takwīn*): when He wills a thing, it is.

﴿عالِيَهُمْ ثِيابُ سُندُسٍ﴾: Qatāda, Mujāhid, Ibn Sīrīn, ʿAwn al-ʿUqaylī, Ibn Muḥayṣ, Abū Jaʿfar, Nāfiʿ, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza, and Ayyūb read *ʿāliyahum* with sukūn on the *yāʾ*, as a named noun described by the verb: *ʿalāhum*, so he is *ʿāliyahum*. Abū ʿUbayd preferred this, on the basis of the reading of Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn Wathhāb and others: *ʿāliyatahum*. Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation: Have you not seen a man wearing garments, with better ones over them? The rest of the readers read it with fatḥa on the *yāʾ*, as an adjective, meaning "above them," and this is the accusative of place (*naṣb ʿalā al-ẓarf*). It was also said: it is like His saying ﴿لاهِيَةً قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾ (their hearts are heedless). [[Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ: 3.]] We have already mentioned this, the placing of the adjective before the noun it describes. It was also said: the meaning is "high for them, its garments," like His saying ﴿هَدْياً بالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ﴾ (an offering reaching the Kaʿba) [[Sūrat al-Māʾida: 95.]] and similar.

﴿خُضْرٌ وَإِسْتَبْرَقٌ﴾: The readers differed about these. Ibn Kathīr, Abū Bakr, and al-Mufaḍḍal read *khuḍrin* in the genitive as a qualifier of *sundus*, and *istabraqun* in the nominative as a qualifier of *thiyāb*. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb read the reverse, and Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred it. Nāfiʿ, Ayyūb, and Ḥafṣ read both in the nominative. Yaḥyā, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read both in the genitive.

﴿وَحُلُّوا أَساوِرَ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾: *ṭahūr* means pure from defilements, which no hands have soiled and no feet have soiled, unlike the wine of this world. Abū Qilāba and Ibrāhīm said: this means it never becomes impure, but turns into a sweat in their hands like the scent of musk. A man of the people of Paradise is granted the appetite of a hundred men of this world, with their eating and craving. When he has eaten what he wishes, he is given a pure drink, which purifies his belly, and what he has eaten becomes a sweat that comes out of his skin, more fragrant than the pungent musk, and his belly shrinks, and his appetite returns. It was also said: it purifies them from sins, impurities, and filth, and makes them sweat for Paradise.

Jaʿfar said: He purifies them through it from everything other than Him, since nothing that has been soiled by the created world is pure.

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: their Lord gave them to drink upon the edge of the carpet of affection. He quenched them from the companionship of creatures and showed them the vision of the Real. Then He seated them upon the pulpits of holiness, greeted them with the greeting of the one who is consoled (*al-muzammil*), and rained down support upon them, so the valleys of longing flowed over them. He removed from them the cares of separation and greeted them with the joy of nearness.

I heard Abū al-Qāsim al-Ḥabībī say: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allah Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Shāshī say: I heard al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlawiyya al-Dāmaghānī say: Abū Yazīd al-Biṣṭāmī was asked about His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾. He said: He purified them through it from love for anything other than Him. Then he said: God has a drink which He has stored for His choicest servants. He Himself undertakes to give them to drink. When they drink, they become intoxicated; when they become intoxicated, they fly; when they fly, they arrive; and when they arrive, they are joined. ﴿فِي مَقْعَدِ صِدْقٍ عِنْدَ مَلِيكٍ مُقْتَدِرٍ﴾ (in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful).

I heard Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī say: I heard Abū Bakr al-Rāzī say: I heard Ṭayyib al-Ḥammāl say: I prayed behind Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah the ʿatama (night) prayer. He recited ﴿وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾, and began moving his mouth as if he were sucking. When he finished his prayer, he was asked: Are you drinking or reciting? He said: By God, if I did not find its pleasure in its recitation like my pleasure in drinking it, I would not have recited it.

Al-Ḥusayn told me, who said: Hārūn told us, who said: Ḥāzim ibn Yaḥyā al-Ḥulwānī told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmmār al-Mawṣilī told us, who said: ʿAfīf ibn Sālim told us, from Ayyūb ibn ʿUtba, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: A man from Abyssinia came to the Prophet (peace be upon him) asking him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "Ask and seek understanding."

He said: O Messenger of God, you have been preferred over us in appearance, colours, and prophethood. Tell me: if I believe in what you believe and act as you act, shall I be with you in Paradise? He said: "Yes." Then the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the whiteness of the black man will be seen in Paradise from a distance of a thousand years." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says: There is no god but God, has a covenant with God through it. And whoever says: Glory be to God and praise be to Him, a hundred thousand good deeds and twenty-four thousand good deeds are written for him."

A man said: How shall we perish after these, O Messenger of God?

He said: "A man will come on the Day of Resurrection, and if it were placed upon a mountain it would weigh it down. Then a blessing from the blessings of God, glory be to Him, will stand up and nearly consume all of that, unless God, exalted be He, shows him favour (*yatawwal*) through His mercy." [[According to Ibn Kathīr: *yataghammadahu* (covers him); according to al-Qurṭubī: *yalṭuf* (is gentle).]] He said: Then the verses were revealed: ﴿هَلْ أَتى عَلَى الْإِنْسانِ حِينٌ مِنَ الدَّهْرِ﴾ up to His saying ﴿وَمُلْكاً كَبِيراً﴾, the verses.

The Abyssinian said: And will my eyes see what your eyes see in Paradise?

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Yes." The Abyssinian then fell ill until his soul departed. Ibn ʿUmar said: I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) lower him into his grave with his own hand. [[Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr: 1/536, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/148.]]

﴿إِنَّ هذا كانَ لَكُمْ جَزاءً وَكانَ سَعْيُكُمْ مَشْكُوراً إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنا عَلَيْكَ الْقُرْآنَ تَنْزِيلًا﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: [It was revealed] in pieces, one verse after another, and He did not send it down all at once; that is why He said ﴿نَزَّلْنا﴾ (We sent down) ...

﴿فَاصْبِرْ لِحُكْمِ رَبِّكَ وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ آثِماً أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾: meaning "or ungrateful (*kafūran*)." The *alif* is an extension (*ṣila*). Al-Farrāʾ said: *aw* here carries the sense of [....] [[Illegible in the manuscript.]], like the saying of the poet:

*No grief of a bereaved mother is like my grief, nor the grief of a bereaved camel whose young has been lost to her.*

*Nor the grief of an old man who lost his she-camel on the day the pilgrims arrive and disperse.*

He meant: "nor the grief of an old man."

Qatāda said: *al-āthim* is *al-kafūr* (the ungrateful). God, exalted be He, forbade His Prophet from obeying Abū Jahl when the prayer was made obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ), while he was still in Makkah. Abū Jahl forbade him from it and said: If I see Muhammad praying, I will step on his neck. So God revealed this verse.

Muqātil said: ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ﴾ means from the polytheists of Makkah, that is ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): If you have done what you have done for the sake of women, Quraysh knows that my daughters are among the most beautiful. I will marry you to my daughter and bring her to you without a dowry, and you will return from this affair. [[Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/149, which has a continuation.]]

﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ means al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): O Muhammad, if you have done this for the sake of wealth, Quraysh knows that I am among the wealthiest of them. I will give you enough wealth to satisfy you, so return from this affair. God, exalted be He, then revealed ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ [آثِماً]﴾, meaning ʿUtba, ﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ meaning and not the ungrateful one, who is al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 76, verses 14–24:**

﴿وَدانِيَةً عَلَيْهِمْ ظِلالُها﴾ means: its shades, the shade of its trees, will be close to them. There are several views on the grammatical case (i'rab) of *dāniyatan*. First, it is coordinated (*'atf*) with the preceding word *muttaki'īna* (reclining). Second, it is coordinated with the position (*mawdi'*) of the phrase ﴿لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها شَمْساً﴾ (they will not see in it a sun), so that the sense is "and they will see [shades] close." Third, it is in the accusative of praise (*al-madh*). The feminine form *dāniyatan* is used because *ẓilāl* (shades) is a plural noun. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿūd), it is *wa-dāniyan ʿalayhim*, which places the verb first. In the codex of Ubayy, it is *wa-dānin*, in the nominative, as a new sentence (*isti'nāf*).

﴿وَذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلًا﴾: *dhullilat* means it was made subservient and brought near. *Quṭūfuhā* means its fruits, and *tadhlīlan* means in complete submission. They will eat from its fruits standing, sitting, and reclining, and they will reach them and take them however they wish, in whatever state they are in.

We were told by ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥāmid, who said: Ḥāmid ibn Muḥammad told us, who said: Mūsā ibn Isḥāq told us, who said: My father told us, who said: Sufyān told us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said: The land of Paradise is of silver (*warq*), its soil is musk, the roots of its trees are gold and silver, its branches are pearls, chrysolite and rubies, and the leaves and fruit are beneath that. Whoever eats standing will not be harmed, [and whoever eats sitting will not be harmed], and whoever eats reclining will not be harmed. That is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿وَذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلًا﴾.

﴿وَيُطافُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِآنِيَةٍ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ وَأَكْوابٍ كانَتْ قَوارِيرَا قَوارِيرَا مِنْ فِضَّةٍ﴾: The commentators said: He meant the whiteness of silver combined with the clarity of glass. Its clarity is that of glass, yet it is made of silver. [[Al-Muṣannaf of Ibn Abī Shayba: 8/67, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/139, at the verse.]]

We were told by Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥamdūn, who said: Makkī told us, who said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Bishr told us, who said: Sufyān told us. And ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥāmid told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ḥamdawayh told us, who said: Maḥmūd ibn Ādam told us, who said: Sufyān told us, from ʿAmr, from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿قَوارِيرَا مِنْ فِضَّةٍ﴾. He said: If you took silver from the silver of this world and beat it until you made it like the wing of a fly, you would not see the water behind it. But the glass of Paradise has the whiteness of silver and the clarity of glass.

Al-Kalbī and al-Thumālī said: God made the glass of each people from the soil of their land. The soil of Paradise is silver, so from that silver He made glasses for them to drink from. ﴿قَدَّرُوها تَقْدِيراً﴾ means they are measured according to their ranks, neither more nor less. Al-Rabīʿ and al-Qurṭubī said: according to the size of the palm. The common reading (*qirā'at al-ʿāmma*, the reading of the majority) has *qaddarahā* with fatḥa on the *qāf* and *dāl*, meaning that the cup-bearers who circulate among them measure it out for them.

He said: He purified them through it from love for anything other than Him. Then he said: God has a drink which He has stored for His choicest servants. He Himself undertakes to give them to drink. When they drink, they become intoxicated; when they become intoxicated, they fly; when they fly, they arrive; and when they arrive, they are joined. ﴿فِي مَقْعَدِ صِدْقٍ عِنْدَ مَلِيكٍ مُقْتَدِرٍ﴾ (in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful).

I heard Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī say: I heard Abū Bakr al-Rāzī say: I heard Ṭayyib al-Ḥammāl say: I prayed behind Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah the ʿatama (night) prayer. He recited ﴿وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾, and began moving his mouth as if he were sucking. When he finished his prayer, he was asked: Are you drinking or reciting? He said: By God, if I did not find its pleasure in its recitation like my pleasure in drinking it, I would not have recited it.

Al-Ḥusayn told me, who said: Hārūn told us, who said: Ḥāzim ibn Yaḥyā al-Ḥulwānī told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmmār al-Mawṣilī told us, who said: ʿAfīf ibn Sālim told us, from Ayyūb ibn ʿUtba, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: A man from Abyssinia came to the Prophet (peace be upon him) asking him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "Ask and seek understanding."

He said: O Messenger of God, you have been preferred over us in appearance, colours, and prophethood. Tell me: if I believe in what you believe and act as you act, shall I be with you in Paradise? He said: "Yes." Then the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the whiteness of the black man will be seen in Paradise from a distance of a thousand years." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says: There is no god but God, has a covenant with God through it. And whoever says: Glory be to God and praise be to Him, a hundred thousand good deeds and twenty-four thousand good deeds are written for him."

A man said: How shall we perish after these, O Messenger of God?

He said: "A man will come on the Day of Resurrection, and if it were placed upon a mountain it would weigh it down. Then a blessing from the blessings of God, glory be to Him, will stand up and nearly consume all of that, unless God, exalted be He, shows him favour (*yatawwal*) through His mercy." [[According to Ibn Kathīr: *yataghammadahu* (covers him); according to al-Qurṭubī: *yalṭuf* (is gentle).]] He said: Then the verses were revealed: ﴿هَلْ أَتى عَلَى الْإِنْسانِ حِينٌ مِنَ الدَّهْرِ﴾ up to His saying ﴿وَمُلْكاً كَبِيراً﴾, the verses.

The Abyssinian said: And will my eyes see what your eyes see in Paradise?

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Yes." The Abyssinian then fell ill until his soul departed. Ibn ʿUmar said: I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) lower him into his grave with his own hand. [[Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr: 1/536, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/148.]]

﴿إِنَّ هذا كانَ لَكُمْ جَزاءً وَكانَ سَعْيُكُمْ مَشْكُوراً إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنا عَلَيْكَ الْقُرْآنَ تَنْزِيلًا﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: [It was revealed] in pieces, one verse after another, and He did not send it down all at once; that is why He said ﴿نَزَّلْنا﴾ (We sent down) ...

﴿فَاصْبِرْ لِحُكْمِ رَبِّكَ وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ آثِماً أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾: meaning "or ungrateful (*kafūran*)." The *alif* is an extension (*ṣila*). Al-Farrāʾ said: *aw* here carries the sense of [....] [[Illegible in the manuscript.]], like the saying of the poet:

*No grief of a bereaved mother is like my grief, nor the grief of a bereaved camel whose young has been lost to her.*

*Nor the grief of an old man who lost his she-camel on the day the pilgrims arrive and disperse.*

He meant: "nor the grief of an old man."

Qatāda said: *al-āthim* is *al-kafūr* (the ungrateful). God, exalted be He, forbade His Prophet from obeying Abū Jahl when the prayer was made obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ), while he was still in Makkah. Abū Jahl forbade him from it and said: If I see Muhammad praying, I will step on his neck. So God revealed this verse.

Muqātil said: ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ﴾ means from the polytheists of Makkah, that is ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): If you have done what you have done for the sake of women, Quraysh knows that my daughters are among the most beautiful. I will marry you to my daughter and bring her to you without a dowry, and you will return from this affair. [[Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/149, which has a continuation.]]

﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ means al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): O Muhammad, if you have done this for the sake of wealth, Quraysh knows that I am among the wealthiest of them. I will give you enough wealth to satisfy you, so return from this affair. God, exalted be He, then revealed ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ [آثِماً]﴾, meaning ʿUtba, ﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ meaning and not the ungrateful one, who is al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 76, verses 14–24:**

﴿وَدانِيَةً عَلَيْهِمْ ظِلالُها﴾ means: its shades, the shade of its trees, will be close to them. There are several views on the grammatical case (i'rab) of *dāniyatan*. First, it is coordinated (*'atf*) with the preceding word *muttaki'īna* (reclining). Second, it is coordinated with the position (*mawdi'*) of the phrase ﴿لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها شَمْساً﴾ (they will not see in it a sun), so that the sense is "and they will see [shades] close." Third, it is in the accusative of praise (*al-madh*). The feminine form *dāniyatan* is used because *ẓilāl* (shades) is a plural noun. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿūd), it is *wa-dāniyan ʿalayhim*, which places the verb first. In the codex of Ubayy, it is *wa-dānin*, in the nominative, as a new sentence (*isti'nāf*).

﴿وَذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلًا﴾: *dhullilat* means it was made subservient and brought near. *Quṭūfuhā* means its fruits, and *tadhlīlan* means in complete submission. They will eat from its fruits standing, sitting, and reclining, and they will reach them and take them however they wish, in whatever state they are in.

We were told by ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥāmid, who said: Ḥāmid ibn Muḥammad told us, who said: Mūsā ibn Isḥāq told us, who said: My father told us, who said: Sufyān told us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said: The land of Paradise is of silver (*warq*), its soil is musk, the roots of its trees are gold and silver, its branches are pearls, chrysolite and rubies, and the leaves and fruit are beneath that. Whoever eats standing will not be harmed, [and whoever eats sitting will not be harmed], and whoever eats reclining will not be harmed. That is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿وَذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلًا﴾.

﴿وَيُطافُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِآنِيَةٍ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ وَأَكْوابٍ كانَتْ قَوارِيرَا قَوارِيرَا مِنْ فِضَّةٍ﴾: The commentators said: He meant the whiteness of silver combined with the clarity of glass. Its clarity is that of glass, yet it is made of silver. [[Al-Muṣannaf of Ibn Abī Shayba: 8/67, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/139, at the verse.]]

We were told by Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥamdūn, who said: Makkī told us, who said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Bishr told us, who said: Sufyān told us. And ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥāmid told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ḥamdawayh told us, who said: Maḥmūd ibn Ādam told us, who said: Sufyān told us, from ʿAmr, from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿قَوارِيرَا مِنْ فِضَّةٍ﴾. He said: If you took silver from the silver of this world and beat it until you made it like the wing of a fly, you would not see the water behind it. But the glass of Paradise has the whiteness of silver and the clarity of glass.

Al-Kalbī and al-Thumālī said: God made the glass of each people from the soil of their land. The soil of Paradise is silver, so from that silver He made glasses for them to drink from. ﴿قَدَّرُوها تَقْدِيراً﴾ means they are measured according to their ranks, neither more nor less. Al-Rabīʿ and al-Qurṭubī said: according to the size of the palm. The common reading (*qirā'at al-ʿāmma*, the reading of the majority) has *qaddarahā* with fatḥa on the *qāf* and *dāl*, meaning that the cup-bearers who circulate among them measure it out for them.

Ibn Fanjawayh told me, who said: Ibn Shanba told us, who said: Abū Ḥāmid al-Mustamlī told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ḥātim al-Raqqī told us, who said: Hishām told us, who said: Ismāʿīl ibn Sālim told us, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: I heard him read it *quddirūhā* with *ḍamma* on the *qāf* and *kasra* on the *dāl*, meaning that it was measured out to them, so there is no excess or deficiency in it. He said: I also heard someone else read *qaddarūhā fī anfusihim* (they measured it in their own minds), so it came to them as they had measured it, neither more nor less.

﴿وَيُسْقَوْنَ فِيها كَأْساً كانَ مِزاجُها زَنْجَبِيلًا﴾: a drink of driving and delight, without intoxication. The Arabs favour ginger (*zanjabīl*), and their poet said:

*As if a jinn of ginger had mixed*
*its taste into her mouth, and a fragrant, spreading wine* [[Kitāb al-ʿAyn of al-Farāhīdī: 6/280. The verse is by al-Aʿshā.]]

It was also said: it is a spring in Paradise from which one tastes the flavour of ginger.

Qatāda said: The muqarrabūn (those brought near) drink it pure, and it is mixed for the rest of the people of Paradise.

﴿عَيْناً فِيها تُسَمَّى سَلْسَبِيلًا﴾: Qatāda said: *salsabīl* means smooth, submissive to them; they direct it wherever they wish. Mujāhid said: it is a fast-flowing stream. [[Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī: 29/271, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: (19/142), where it reads: fast-flowing, flowing into their throats with ease.]] Yamān said: it is good in taste and flavour. The Arabs say: this is a smooth (*salis*) and *salsal* and *salsabīl* drink. Abū al-ʿĀliya and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said: it was named *salsabīl* because it flows smoothly over them in the paths and in their dwellings. It springs from the root of the Throne, from the Garden of Eden, to the people of the gardens, with the coldness of camphor, the taste of ginger, and the scent of musk. The meaning of *tusammā* (is named) is "is described," because most scholars hold that *salsabīl* is a descriptive attribute of the name.

﴿وَيَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ وِلْدانٌ مُخَلَّدُونَ إِذا رَأَيْتَهُمْ حَسِبْتَهُمْ لُؤْلُؤاً مَنْثُوراً وَإِذا رَأَيْتَ ثَمَّ رَأَيْتَ نَعِيماً وَمُلْكاً كَبِيراً﴾. The meaning of *mulkan kabīran* is that the lowest of them in rank (meaning the people of Paradise) will look from his kingdom across a distance of a thousand years, and will see its farthest end as clearly as its nearest. It was also said: it is the angels' seeking permission to enter upon them. And it was said: *mulkan kabīran* means a kingdom that has no end.

Abū Bakr al-Warrāq said: a kingdom not followed by destruction. Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Tirmidhī said: it means the kingdom of creation (*mulk al-takwīn*): when He wills a thing, it is.

﴿عالِيَهُمْ ثِيابُ سُندُسٍ﴾: Qatāda, Mujāhid, Ibn Sīrīn, ʿAwn al-ʿUqaylī, Ibn Muḥayṣ, Abū Jaʿfar, Nāfiʿ, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza, and Ayyūb read *ʿāliyahum* with sukūn on the *yāʾ*, as a named noun described by the verb: *ʿalāhum*, so he is *ʿāliyahum*. Abū ʿUbayd preferred this, on the basis of the reading of Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn Wathhāb and others: *ʿāliyatahum*. Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation: Have you not seen a man wearing garments, with better ones over them? The rest of the readers read it with fatḥa on the *yāʾ*, as an adjective, meaning "above them," and this is the accusative of place (*naṣb ʿalā al-ẓarf*). It was also said: it is like His saying ﴿لاهِيَةً قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾ (their hearts are heedless). [[Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ: 3.]] We have already mentioned this, the placing of the adjective before the noun it describes. It was also said: the meaning is "high for them, its garments," like His saying ﴿هَدْياً بالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ﴾ (an offering reaching the Kaʿba) [[Sūrat al-Māʾida: 95.]] and similar.

﴿خُضْرٌ وَإِسْتَبْرَقٌ﴾: The readers differed about these. Ibn Kathīr, Abū Bakr, and al-Mufaḍḍal read *khuḍrin* in the genitive as a qualifier of *sundus*, and *istabraqun* in the nominative as a qualifier of *thiyāb*. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb read the reverse, and Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred it. Nāfiʿ, Ayyūb, and Ḥafṣ read both in the nominative. Yaḥyā, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read both in the genitive.

﴿وَحُلُّوا أَساوِرَ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾: *ṭahūr* means pure from defilements, which no hands have soiled and no feet have soiled, unlike the wine of this world. Abū Qilāba and Ibrāhīm said: this means it never becomes impure, but turns into a sweat in their hands like the scent of musk. A man of the people of Paradise is granted the appetite of a hundred men of this world, with their eating and craving. When he has eaten what he wishes, he is given a pure drink, which purifies his belly, and what he has eaten becomes a sweat that comes out of his skin, more fragrant than the pungent musk, and his belly shrinks, and his appetite returns. It was also said: it purifies them from sins, impurities, and filth, and makes them sweat for Paradise.

Jaʿfar said: He purifies them through it from everything other than Him, since nothing that has been soiled by the created world is pure.

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: their Lord gave them to drink upon the edge of the carpet of affection. He quenched them from the companionship of creatures and showed them the vision of the Real. Then He seated them upon the pulpits of holiness, greeted them with the greeting of the one who is consoled (*al-muzammil*), and rained down support upon them, so the valleys of longing flowed over them. He removed from them the cares of separation and greeted them with the joy of nearness.

I heard Abū al-Qāsim al-Ḥabībī say: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allah Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Shāshī say: I heard al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlawiyya al-Dāmaghānī say: Abū Yazīd al-Biṣṭāmī was asked about His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾. He said: He purified them through it from love for anything other than Him. Then he said: God has a drink which He has stored for His choicest servants. He Himself undertakes to give them to drink. When they drink, they become intoxicated; when they become intoxicated, they fly; when they fly, they arrive; and when they arrive, they are joined. ﴿فِي مَقْعَدِ صِدْقٍ عِنْدَ مَلِيكٍ مُقْتَدِرٍ﴾ (in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful).

I heard Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī say: I heard Abū Bakr al-Rāzī say: I heard Ṭayyib al-Ḥammāl say: I prayed behind Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah the ʿatama (night) prayer. He recited ﴿وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾, and began moving his mouth as if he were sucking. When he finished his prayer, he was asked: Are you drinking or reciting? He said: By God, if I did not find its pleasure in its recitation like my pleasure in drinking it, I would not have recited it.

Al-Ḥusayn told me, who said: Hārūn told us, who said: Ḥāzim ibn Yaḥyā al-Ḥulwānī told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmmār al-Mawṣilī told us, who said: ʿAfīf ibn Sālim told us, from Ayyūb ibn ʿUtba, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: A man from Abyssinia came to the Prophet (peace be upon him) asking him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "Ask and seek understanding."

He said: O Messenger of God, you have been preferred over us in appearance, colours, and prophethood. Tell me: if I believe in what you believe and act as you act, shall I be with you in Paradise? He said: "Yes." Then the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the whiteness of the black man will be seen in Paradise from a distance of a thousand years." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says: There is no god but God, has a covenant with God through it. And whoever says: Glory be to God and praise be to Him, a hundred thousand good deeds and twenty-four thousand good deeds are written for him."

A man said: How shall we perish after these, O Messenger of God?

He said: "A man will come on the Day of Resurrection, and if it were placed upon a mountain it would weigh it down. Then a blessing from the blessings of God, glory be to Him, will stand up and nearly consume all of that, unless God, exalted be He, shows him favour (*yatawwal*) through His mercy." [[According to Ibn Kathīr: *yataghammadahu* (covers him); according to al-Qurṭubī: *yalṭuf* (is gentle).]] He said: Then the verses were revealed: ﴿هَلْ أَتى عَلَى الْإِنْسانِ حِينٌ مِنَ الدَّهْرِ﴾ up to His saying ﴿وَمُلْكاً كَبِيراً﴾, the verses.

The Abyssinian said: And will my eyes see what your eyes see in Paradise?

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Yes." The Abyssinian then fell ill until his soul departed. Ibn ʿUmar said: I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) lower him into his grave with his own hand. [[Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr: 1/536, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/148.]]

﴿إِنَّ هذا كانَ لَكُمْ جَزاءً وَكانَ سَعْيُكُمْ مَشْكُوراً إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنا عَلَيْكَ الْقُرْآنَ تَنْزِيلًا﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: [It was revealed] in pieces, one verse after another, and He did not send it down all at once; that is why He said ﴿نَزَّلْنا﴾ (We sent down) ...

﴿فَاصْبِرْ لِحُكْمِ رَبِّكَ وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ آثِماً أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾: meaning "or ungrateful (*kafūran*)." The *alif* is an extension (*ṣila*). Al-Farrāʾ said: *aw* here carries the sense of [....] [[Illegible in the manuscript.]], like the saying of the poet:

*No grief of a bereaved mother is like my grief, nor the grief of a bereaved camel whose young has been lost to her.*

*Nor the grief of an old man who lost his she-camel on the day the pilgrims arrive and disperse.*

He meant: "nor the grief of an old man."

Qatāda said: *al-āthim* is *al-kafūr* (the ungrateful). God, exalted be He, forbade His Prophet from obeying Abū Jahl when the prayer was made obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ), while he was still in Makkah. Abū Jahl forbade him from it and said: If I see Muhammad praying, I will step on his neck. So God revealed this verse.

Muqātil said: ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ﴾ means from the polytheists of Makkah, that is ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): If you have done what you have done for the sake of women, Quraysh knows that my daughters are among the most beautiful. I will marry you to my daughter and bring her to you without a dowry, and you will return from this affair. [[Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/149, which has a continuation.]]

﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ means al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): O Muhammad, if you have done this for the sake of wealth, Quraysh knows that I am among the wealthiest of them. I will give you enough wealth to satisfy you, so return from this affair. God, exalted be He, then revealed ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ [آثِماً]﴾, meaning ʿUtba, ﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ meaning and not the ungrateful one, who is al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 76, verses 14–24:**

﴿وَدانِيَةً عَلَيْهِمْ ظِلالُها﴾ means: its shades, the shade of its trees, will be close to them. There are several views on the grammatical case (i'rab) of *dāniyatan*. First, it is coordinated (*'atf*) with the preceding word *muttaki'īna* (reclining). Second, it is coordinated with the position (*mawdi'*) of the phrase ﴿لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها شَمْساً﴾ (they will not see in it a sun), so that the sense is "and they will see [shades] close." Third, it is in the accusative of praise (*al-madh*). The feminine form *dāniyatan* is used because *ẓilāl* (shades) is a plural noun. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿūd), it is *wa-dāniyan ʿalayhim*, which places the verb first. In the codex of Ubayy, it is *wa-dānin*, in the nominative, as a new sentence (*isti'nāf*).

﴿وَذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلًا﴾: *dhullilat* means it was made subservient and brought near. *Quṭūfuhā* means its fruits, and *tadhlīlan* means in complete submission. They will eat from its fruits standing, sitting, and reclining, and they will reach them and take them however they wish, in whatever state they are in.

We were told by ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥāmid, who said: Ḥāmid ibn Muḥammad told us, who said: Mūsā ibn Isḥāq told us, who said: My father told us, who said: Sufyān told us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said: The land of Paradise is of silver (*warq*), its soil is musk, the roots of its trees are gold and silver, its branches are pearls, chrysolite and rubies, and the leaves and fruit are beneath that. Whoever eats standing will not be harmed, [and whoever eats sitting will not be harmed], and whoever eats reclining will not be harmed. That is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿وَذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلًا﴾.

﴿وَيُطافُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِآنِيَةٍ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ وَأَكْوابٍ كانَتْ قَوارِيرَا قَوارِيرَا مِنْ فِضَّةٍ﴾: The commentators said: He meant the whiteness of silver combined with the clarity of glass. Its clarity is that of glass, yet it is made of silver. [[Al-Muṣannaf of Ibn Abī Shayba: 8/67, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/139, at the verse.]]

We were told by Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥamdūn, who said: Makkī told us, who said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Bishr told us, who said: Sufyān told us. And ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥāmid told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ḥamdawayh told us, who said: Maḥmūd ibn Ādam told us, who said: Sufyān told us, from ʿAmr, from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿قَوارِيرَا مِنْ فِضَّةٍ﴾. He said: If you took silver from the silver of this world and beat it until you made it like the wing of a fly, you would not see the water behind it. But the glass of Paradise has the whiteness of silver and the clarity of glass.

Al-Kalbī and al-Thumālī said: God made the glass of each people from the soil of their land. The soil of Paradise is silver, so from that silver He made glasses for them to drink from. ﴿قَدَّرُوها تَقْدِيراً﴾ means they are measured according to their ranks, neither more nor less. Al-Rabīʿ and al-Qurṭubī said: according to the size of the palm. The common reading (*qirā'at al-ʿāmma*, the reading of the majority) has *qaddarahā* with fatḥa on the *qāf* and *dāl*, meaning that the cup-bearers who circulate among them measure it out for them.

Ibn Fanjawayh told me, who said: Ibn Shanba told us, who said: Abū Ḥāmid al-Mustamlī told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ḥātim al-Raqqī told us, who said: Hishām told us, who said: Ismāʿīl ibn Sālim told us, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: I heard him read it *quddirūhā* with *ḍamma* on the *qāf* and *kasra* on the *dāl*, meaning that it was measured out to them, so there is no excess or deficiency in it. He said: I also heard someone else read *qaddarūhā fī anfusihim* (they measured it in their own minds), so it came to them as they had measured it, neither more nor less.

﴿وَيُسْقَوْنَ فِيها كَأْساً كانَ مِزاجُها زَنْجَبِيلًا﴾: a drink of driving and delight, without intoxication. The Arabs favour ginger (*zanjabīl*), and their poet said:

*As if a jinn of ginger had mixed*
*its taste into her mouth, and a fragrant, spreading wine* [[Kitāb al-ʿAyn of al-Farāhīdī: 6/280. The verse is by al-Aʿshā.]]

It was also said: it is a spring in Paradise from which one tastes the flavour of ginger.

Qatāda said: The muqarrabūn (those brought near) drink it pure, and it is mixed for the rest of the people of Paradise.

﴿عَيْناً فِيها تُسَمَّى سَلْسَبِيلًا﴾: Qatāda said: *salsabīl* means smooth, submissive to them; they direct it wherever they wish. Mujāhid said: it is a fast-flowing stream. [[Tafsīr al-Ṭabarī: 29/271, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: (19/142), where it reads: fast-flowing, flowing into their throats with ease.]] Yamān said: it is good in taste and flavour. The Arabs say: this is a smooth (*salis*) and *salsal* and *salsabīl* drink. Abū al-ʿĀliya and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said: it was named *salsabīl* because it flows smoothly over them in the paths and in their dwellings. It springs from the root of the Throne, from the Garden of Eden, to the people of the gardens, with the coldness of camphor, the taste of ginger, and the scent of musk. The meaning of *tusammā* (is named) is "is described," because most scholars hold that *salsabīl* is a descriptive attribute of the name.

﴿وَيَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ وِلْدانٌ مُخَلَّدُونَ إِذا رَأَيْتَهُمْ حَسِبْتَهُمْ لُؤْلُؤاً مَنْثُوراً وَإِذا رَأَيْتَ ثَمَّ رَأَيْتَ نَعِيماً وَمُلْكاً كَبِيراً﴾. The meaning of *mulkan kabīran* is that the lowest of them in rank (meaning the people of Paradise) will look from his kingdom across a distance of a thousand years, and will see its farthest end as clearly as its nearest. It was also said: it is the angels' seeking permission to enter upon them. And it was said: *mulkan kabīran* means a kingdom that has no end.

Abū Bakr al-Warrāq said: a kingdom not followed by destruction. Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Tirmidhī said: it means the kingdom of creation (*mulk al-takwīn*): when He wills a thing, it is.

﴿عالِيَهُمْ ثِيابُ سُندُسٍ﴾: Qatāda, Mujāhid, Ibn Sīrīn, ʿAwn al-ʿUqaylī, Ibn Muḥayṣ, Abū Jaʿfar, Nāfiʿ, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza, and Ayyūb read *ʿāliyahum* with sukūn on the *yāʾ*, as a named noun described by the verb: *ʿalāhum*, so he is *ʿāliyahum*. Abū ʿUbayd preferred this, on the basis of the reading of Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn Wathhāb and others: *ʿāliyatahum*. Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation: Have you not seen a man wearing garments, with better ones over them? The rest of the readers read it with fatḥa on the *yāʾ*, as an adjective, meaning "above them," and this is the accusative of place (*naṣb ʿalā al-ẓarf*). It was also said: it is like His saying ﴿لاهِيَةً قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾ (their hearts are heedless). [[Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ: 3.]] We have already mentioned this, the placing of the adjective before the noun it describes. It was also said: the meaning is "high for them, its garments," like His saying ﴿هَدْياً بالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ﴾ (an offering reaching the Kaʿba) [[Sūrat al-Māʾida: 95.]] and similar.

﴿خُضْرٌ وَإِسْتَبْرَقٌ﴾: The readers differed about these. Ibn Kathīr, Abū Bakr, and al-Mufaḍḍal read *khuḍrin* in the genitive as a qualifier of *sundus*, and *istabraqun* in the nominative as a qualifier of *thiyāb*. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb read the reverse, and Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred it. Nāfiʿ, Ayyūb, and Ḥafṣ read both in the nominative. Yaḥyā, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read both in the genitive.

﴿وَحُلُّوا أَساوِرَ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾: *ṭahūr* means pure from defilements, which no hands have soiled and no feet have soiled, unlike the wine of this world. Abū Qilāba and Ibrāhīm said: this means it never becomes impure, but turns into a sweat in their hands like the scent of musk. A man of the people of Paradise is granted the appetite of a hundred men of this world, with their eating and craving. When he has eaten what he wishes, he is given a pure drink, which purifies his belly, and what he has eaten becomes a sweat that comes out of his skin, more fragrant than the pungent musk, and his belly shrinks, and his appetite returns. It was also said: it purifies them from sins, impurities, and filth, and makes them sweat for Paradise.

Jaʿfar said: He purifies them through it from everything other than Him, since nothing that has been soiled by the created world is pure.

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: their Lord gave them to drink upon the edge of the carpet of affection. He quenched them from the companionship of creatures and showed them the vision of the Real. Then He seated them upon the pulpits of holiness, greeted them with the greeting of the one who is consoled (*al-muzammil*), and rained down support upon them, so the valleys of longing flowed over them. He removed from them the cares of separation and greeted them with the joy of nearness.

I heard Abū al-Qāsim al-Ḥabībī say: I heard Abū ʿAbd Allah Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Shāshī say: I heard al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlawiyya al-Dāmaghānī say: Abū Yazīd al-Biṣṭāmī was asked about His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾. He said: He purified them through it from love for anything other than Him. Then he said: God has a drink which He has stored for His choicest servants. He Himself undertakes to give them to drink. When they drink, they become intoxicated; when they become intoxicated, they fly; when they fly, they arrive; and when they arrive, they are joined. ﴿فِي مَقْعَدِ صِدْقٍ عِنْدَ مَلِيكٍ مُقْتَدِرٍ﴾ (in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful).

I heard Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī say: I heard Abū Bakr al-Rāzī say: I heard Ṭayyib al-Ḥammāl say: I prayed behind Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah the ʿatama (night) prayer. He recited ﴿وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾, and began moving his mouth as if he were sucking. When he finished his prayer, he was asked: Are you drinking or reciting? He said: By God, if I did not find its pleasure in its recitation like my pleasure in drinking it, I would not have recited it.

Al-Ḥusayn told me, who said: Hārūn told us, who said: Ḥāzim ibn Yaḥyā al-Ḥulwānī told us, who said: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmmār al-Mawṣilī told us, who said: ʿAfīf ibn Sālim told us, from Ayyūb ibn ʿUtba, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: A man from Abyssinia came to the Prophet (peace be upon him) asking him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "Ask and seek understanding."

He said: O Messenger of God, you have been preferred over us in appearance, colours, and prophethood. Tell me: if I believe in what you believe and act as you act, shall I be with you in Paradise? He said: "Yes." Then the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the whiteness of the black man will be seen in Paradise from a distance of a thousand years." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says: There is no god but God, has a covenant with God through it. And whoever says: Glory be to God and praise be to Him, a hundred thousand good deeds and twenty-four thousand good deeds are written for him."

A man said: How shall we perish after these, O Messenger of God?

He said: "A man will come on the Day of Resurrection, and if it were placed upon a mountain it would weigh it down. Then a blessing from the blessings of God, glory be to Him, will stand up and nearly consume all of that, unless God, exalted be He, shows him favour (*yatawwal*) through His mercy." [[According to Ibn Kathīr: *yataghammadahu* (covers him); according to al-Qurṭubī: *yalṭuf* (is gentle).]] He said: Then the verses were revealed: ﴿هَلْ أَتى عَلَى الْإِنْسانِ حِينٌ مِنَ الدَّهْرِ﴾ up to His saying ﴿وَمُلْكاً كَبِيراً﴾, the verses.

The Abyssinian said: And will my eyes see what your eyes see in Paradise?

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Yes." The Abyssinian then fell ill until his soul departed. Ibn ʿUmar said: I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) lower him into his grave with his own hand. [[Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr: 1/536, and Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/148.]]

﴿إِنَّ هذا كانَ لَكُمْ جَزاءً وَكانَ سَعْيُكُمْ مَشْكُوراً إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنا عَلَيْكَ الْقُرْآنَ تَنْزِيلًا﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: [It was revealed] in pieces, one verse after another, and He did not send it down all at once; that is why He said ﴿نَزَّلْنا﴾ (We sent down) ...

﴿فَاصْبِرْ لِحُكْمِ رَبِّكَ وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ آثِماً أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾: meaning "or ungrateful (*kafūran*)." The *alif* is an extension (*ṣila*). Al-Farrāʾ said: *aw* here carries the sense of [....] [[Illegible in the manuscript.]], like the saying of the poet:

*No grief of a bereaved mother is like my grief, nor the grief of a bereaved camel whose young has been lost to her.*

*Nor the grief of an old man who lost his she-camel on the day the pilgrims arrive and disperse.*

He meant: "nor the grief of an old man."

Qatāda said: *al-āthim* is *al-kafūr* (the ungrateful). God, exalted be He, forbade His Prophet from obeying Abū Jahl when the prayer was made obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ), while he was still in Makkah. Abū Jahl forbade him from it and said: If I see Muhammad praying, I will step on his neck. So God revealed this verse.

Muqātil said: ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ﴾ means from the polytheists of Makkah, that is ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): If you have done what you have done for the sake of women, Quraysh knows that my daughters are among the most beautiful. I will marry you to my daughter and bring her to you without a dowry, and you will return from this affair. [[Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 19/149, which has a continuation.]]

﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ means al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): O Muhammad, if you have done this for the sake of wealth, Quraysh knows that I am among the wealthiest of them. I will give you enough wealth to satisfy you, so return from this affair. God, exalted be He, then revealed ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ [آثِماً]﴾, meaning ʿUtba, ﴿أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾ meaning and not the ungrateful one, who is al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 76, verses 14–24:**

﴿وَدانِيَةً عَلَيْهِمْ ظِلالُها﴾ means: its shades, the shade of its trees, will be close to them. There are several views on the grammatical case (i'rab) of *dāniyatan*. First, it is coordinated (*'atf*) with the preceding word *muttaki'īna* (reclining). Second, it is coordinated with the position (*mawdi'*) of the phrase ﴿لا يَرَوْنَ فِيها شَمْساً﴾ (they will not see in it a sun), so that the sense is "and they will see [shades] close." Third, it is in the accusative of praise (*al-madh*). The feminine form *dāniyatan* is used because *ẓilāl* (shades) is a plural noun. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿūd), it is *wa-dāniyan ʿalayhim*, which places the verb first. In the codex of Ubayy, it is *wa-dānin*, in the nominative, as a new sentence (*isti'nāf*).

﴿وَذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلًا﴾: *dhullilat* means it was made subservient and brought near. *Quṭūfuhā* means its fruits, and *tadhlīlan* means in complete submission. They will eat from its fruits standing, sitting, and reclining, and they will reach them and take them however they wish, in whatever state they are in.

We were told by ʿAbd Allah ibn Ḥāmid, who said: Ḥāmid ibn Muḥammad told us, who said: Mūsā ibn Isḥāq told us, who said: My father told us, who said: Sufyān told us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said: The land of Paradise is of silver (*warq*), its soil is musk, the roots of its trees are gold and silver, its branches are pearls, chrysolite and rubies, and the leaves and fruit are beneath that.
